title: Baba Farid Sings Punjabi
subtitle: How a Chishti saint’s rough village tongue became a river of song
region: Multan, Hansi and Ajodhan or Pakpattan
moral: A mother tongue can carry the highest longing.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Baba Farid slokas, compiled 1604
sources.note: Strong textual anchor for the Farid verse tradition.

sources.citation: Mir Khord, Siyar al-Auliya, c. 1350; Hasan Sijzi, Fawa'id al-Fu'wad
sources.note: Chishti lineage sources connecting Farid to Nizamuddin Auliya.

sources.citation: K.A. Nizami, The Life and Times of Shaikh Farid-ud-Din Ganj-i-Shakar (1973); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Historical context for Punjab, Chishti institutions and scripture.

panels.shot: wide, dusk-lit view of Baba Farid seated on a simple mat by the Sutlej, silhouettes of villagers listening as fields stretch into haze

dialogue.text: In an age of Persian courts and Arabic law, Baba Farid of Ajodhan let the villages speak—and his rough-hewn couplets still echo in scripture centuries later.

panels.shot: slow push-in from high above a caravan road between Multan and Delhi, fading into a close on Farid walking with a staff

dialogue.text: Farid-ud-Din Masud, later called Ganj-i-Shakar, lived between worlds—Multan’s Sufi circles, Hansi’s teachers, and the long road to Ajodhan in the thirteenth-century Delhi Sultanate.

panels.shot: interior medium shot in a modest study-room in Multan, low-angle on a young Farid copying Arabic on a palm-leaf or paper

dialogue.text: Born into a family touched by learning and piety, Farid’s early path ran through Arabic prayers, Persian texts and the disciplined training of the Chishti Sufi order.

panels.shot: close-up on Farid’s attentive face in a khanqah at Hansi, with an elder Chishti saint in soft focus teaching disciples

dialogue.text: The Siyar al-Auliya and Fawa’id al-Fu’wad remember him as a key link in the Chishti chain—teacher to Nizamuddin Auliya’s generation, shaping ways of devotion more than courts or armies.

panels.shot: wide shot of Ajodhan/Pakpattan town and surrounding fields, khanqah visible as a humble complex on the edge

dialogue.text: When Farid settled at Ajodhan—later Pakpattan—he chose not a capital, but a river town on the frontier of Punjab, where farmers, traders and wanderers passed in endless streams.

panels.shot: interior wide of the Pakpattan khanqah courtyard, with cooking hearths and travelers seated in rows eating

dialogue.text: The Chishti khanqah at Pakpattan became a house of hospitality—bread and comfort for strangers, a node in the networks of travel that stitched Multan, Lahore and Delhi together.

panels.shot: close-up on Farid listening at the doorway to two farmers chatting in a thick local dialect

dialogue.text: Here Farid measured the pulse of the countryside—their speech rough, mixed with Multani and Punjabi forms, their anxieties far from the polished Persian of sultans and scholars.

panels.shot: medium shot of a teaching circle, Farid addressing villagers and disciples seated on mats

dialogue.speaker: baba_farid
dialogue.text: If their hearts are in this tongue, must not God’s remembrance flow in it too?

panels.shot: tight close-up on Farid’s mouth as he recites a couplet, background blurred villagers listening

dialogue.text: So the saint began to shape brief couplets in their own speech—short slokas on loss, humility and longing, spoken not in courtly Persian but in the idiom of the fields.

panels.shot: medium shot of a villager wiping eyes, moved by the verse, with Farid serene in the background

dialogue.text: The words were simple, but the impact deep—daily sorrow turned into prayer, the ache of separation framed as a path back to the Beloved.

panels.shot: interior close-up on a disciple’s hand writing lines on rough paper, Farid’s voice heard off-frame

dialogue.text: Some disciples carried these sayings onward, memorizing and noting them down. Not all survive, and the verses we have passed through many mouths and pens before reaching us.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye of pilgrims leaving Pakpattan in different directions, carrying the words with them

dialogue.text: Along trade routes and pilgrimage paths, Farid’s sayings spread—woven into the oral fabric of Punjab, recited in gatherings far beyond Pakpattan’s mud walls.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of the Pakpattan khanqah under changing skies, hinting at decades passing

dialogue.text: Farid died around 1266. After him, the khanqah continued, and the Chishti line moved on—toward Delhi, toward Nizamuddin Auliya, carrying memories of the saint of Ajodhan.

panels.shot: interior wide of a later Delhi Chishti gathering, with Nizamuddin Auliya teaching, a disciple reciting a Farid verse

dialogue.text: Chishti chronicles like Hasan Sijzi’s Fawa’id al-Fu’wad place Farid within the living chain—his name and sayings honoured among later saints, his style of tenderness admired.

panels.shot: wide shot of Punjab landscape centuries later, with scattered village gatherings where someone recites an old sloka

dialogue.text: Across generations, some of Farid’s verse lived on in oral tradition. Language shifted; dialects changed. Yet certain lines stayed, tied to his name and aura.

panels.shot: interior close-up of hands of Sikh scribes in the early 1600s writing the Guru Granth Sahib, with a folio showing Farid’s name

dialogue.text: In 1604, when the Guru Granth Sahib was compiled, a selection of slokas attributed to Farid found a home there—anchoring his voice within Sikh scripture’s vast chorus.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on the written lines of a Farid sloka, ink slightly faded, script clear

dialogue.text: Scholars note that these verses show a mix of early Punjabi and Multani elements, shaped by centuries of transmission—not identical to modern standard Punjabi, yet unmistakably of the region.

panels.shot: wide, reverent shot of a contemporary Sikh congregation listening as a Granthi recites Farid’s verses

dialogue.text: Today, Farid’s slokas are still sung as part of daily worship—Sufi-born, preserved in Sikh scripture, a reminder of how devotion can cross institutional and communal lines.

panels.shot: final contemplative close-up of Farid at Pakpattan at twilight, fields behind him fading into darkness

dialogue.text: Farid did not seek to adorn the courts; he let the mother tongue of his land carry the highest longing—and in that choice, his quiet village words became an enduring river of prayer.
